newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: FEATURE - UAE thrives on oil, seen facing few threats.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UAE thrives on oil, seen facing few threats.

text.p: When foreign forces withdrew their protection from the Gulf coast of Arabia, few were ready to give the string of sparsely-populated sheikhdoms they left to defend themselves much chance of survival.
The foreigners were the British, whose naval gunboats and civil administrators had provided a shield against attack and a system of rule in the region's coastal villages for 150 years.
In 1971, when Britain was fully engaged in dismantling its colonial empire, they pulled out.

A quarter-century on, the once impoverished Trucial States known for fishing, pearl-diving and a history of tribal feuding thrive as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) -- awash with revenue from oil and gas exports and one of the world's richest states.
The country's silver jubilee is on December 2.
Petrodollars and laissez-faire rule by decree unhindered by party politics have created a modern welfare state with a distinctive bedouin touch and a strong tribal tradition.

Its largely featureless desert landscape is studded with landmark towers in modern cities which compete in keen but amicable rivalry for international business. Schools, hospitals, highways and mosques have transformed a once-barren wasteland.

"The UAE's greatest achievement is that it has lasted 25 years," said a diplomat with long experience of the Gulf. "In 1971 there were plenty of people around who gave it a few months, may be a few years at the most."

"People were very sceptical about the whole idea of a federation," another Gulf-based diplomat said. "There was tremendous focus on rivalry between Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Also, these states are surrounded by big neighbours.
"But they've proved the UAE is a going concern because it's in their own self-interest to hang together rather than hang separately."
Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, ruler of the oil-rich emirate of Abu Dhabi since his brother Shakhbout was deposed in 1966, was named federal president.
Sprightly but frail after recent surgery in the United States, the descendant of the Arabian peninsula's Bani Yas tribe is recognised as the Gulf's elder statesman.
"History will record the great benefits that federation has brought to the emirates as well as to the whole region," says Khalfan bin Mohammad al-Roumi, UAE Information and Culture Minister.
"In Sheikh Zaid's view, it was the only path that could secure stability, strength and prosperity for its people and in this he has been well vindicated."
Although adoption of a permanent constitution was not deemed necessary until this year, diplomats say the federation is a state whose cohesion is all but guaranteed.

Diplomats say it suffers none of the Sunni-Shi'ite religious rows seen elsewhere in the Gulf and has no major internal opposition movements. Barring action by larger regional powers, notably Iran, they forecast stability and yet more prosperity.
"I've lived to see it go from a hardship post to a holiday resort," said one veteran diplomat.
"It's got no debt, no poverty and no dissidents. A very barren, inhospitable coastline has been transformed into very comfortable cities."

The UAE is in dispute with Iran over three islands near sea lanes plied by oil tankers in the strategic Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf and is in the market for a $6 billion fleet of 80 long-range strike aircraft as a deterrent.

Besides Abu Dhabi -- largest, wealthiest and most influential of the seven emirates -- the UAE comprises the Gulf's dynamic trade hub Dubai and the smaller, poorer sheikhdoms of Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain, Ras al-Khaimah and Fujairah, all of whom depend on federal largesse.

Together they comprise an area a little larger than Scotland but with less than half the population. Just over two million people live in the UAE. Only one in four is a national, most others being workers from the Indian subcontinent.
Much of the native population is under 30 -- half under 16 -- so Sheikh Zaid, now 78, is the only leader many have known.
"The greatest danger is of a rapidly expanding young population with high expectations and little prospect of these being fulfilled. That's the priority," one diplomat said.
"Inevitably there will be a lot of pressure on the UAE government to provide decent earnings, and pressure on companies to provide middle-management jobs for Emiratis.

"The external threat is taken very seriously. But it's a difference of perception, led by the amount of day-to-day business done with Iran. Dubai and Sharjah, which do most, argue for a cooperative and constructive relationship with Tehran rather than a confrontational one. This is one of the few issues on which you hear a difference of view."
"Here in Abu Dhabi they are worried sick about the Iranian arms build-up," said another diplomat. "Iran is seen as truculent, difficult and a bit threatening."
